title: A king with no sons

segments.voice: Yesterday: sankat mochan, and a mountain carried through the night. You've met Hanuman. Now, for five weeks, the whole story he lives inside.

Ayodhya. A shining city on a river, with walls and gardens and elephants, and a good king named Dasharatha. His name means ten chariots. He has wealth, peace, and three queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And no son. Year after year, the kingdom waits for an heir, and the king grows old. He has done everything a king can do, and the one thing he wants most has not come. Some waits are like that: what seems to come easily to everyone else just keeps not arriving.

This is the opening of the Ramayana, the story of Rama. Tradition says Valmiki composed it, and calls him the first poet. It's honored as sacred, not only told as a story, and it has been retold in language after language. For the next five weeks, i'll walk you through it, one scene a day, like a serial. Dasharatha's advisers suggest a great fire ritual for the sake of sons, and bring a young sage, Rishyashringa, to lead it. The offerings go in. Out of the flames rises a shining figure carrying a golden bowl of sweet rice pudding, payasa, sent by the gods. Give this to your queens, he says. Dasharatha divides it among the three, and in time, four sons are born. Kausalya bears Rama. Kaikeyi bears Bharata. Sumitra bears twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Four boys, after all those years. The text also tells what the gods are doing behind the scenes: Vishnu, the preserver, has chosen to be born as Rama to deal with a demon king no god can defeat. Remember that, and remember the name Kaikeyi. Notice how it opens. This great epic doesn't begin with a battle or a hero. It begins with a long wait: an old man hoping. And the answer, when it comes, is bigger than what he asked for. He wanted one heir. He got four sons, and one of them changes everything. Some things arrive late.
screen: `THE RAMAYANA: VALMIKI'S STORY.` · `A FIRE, A GOLDEN BOWL.` · `FOUR SONS, THREE QUEENS.` · `IT BEGINS WITH A WAIT.` · then, large: `SOME THINGS ARRIVE LATE.`

segments.voice: Name something you've been waiting for: a job, a healing, a person, a child, a change. Don't pretend it doesn't hurt; let the wanting be there, and breathe with it without asking it to hurry. If you pray, you can hold it up to God; if you don't, just hold it gently, like a bowl.
Putrakameshti, the fire sacrifice for the wish of a son, after years of Dasharatha's waiting. A golden bowl comes from the flames, and four sons are born: Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna.
Your line: some things arrive late. And sometimes they come bigger than the wish. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus read the Ramayana in their own language, recite it at home or in temples, and watch it performed as Ramlila each autumn; Rama's birthday is celebrated as Rama Navami in spring.

original.note: Sanskrit: the sacrifice (ishti) for the desire (kama) of a son (putra).

trapdoor: what you thought: a king has some sons.
what it means: the great epic opens with a long wait, a fire ritual, and four sons, one of them Rama.
what a scholar hears: the putrakameshti, led by Rishyashringa; Valmiki's Bala Kanda also frames Rama as Vishnu taking birth to defeat Ravana.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 8–18 (Dasharatha's wish; the sacrifice; the payasa; the four births)

notes: Fresh editor pass (2026-10-01): cut the verse and book count (the earlier note on 24,000 verses is now moot), 'every Indian language', the superlative 'the greatest story in the tradition', the invented gloss 'could drive in every direction at once', and 'you probably know someone like him. Maybe you are' (told the listener about their life); 'no children' made 'no son' to match the title and Valmiki's framing (some traditions give Dasharatha a daughter, Shanta); replaced the stock turn 'Here's what the story knows'.
About 24,000 verses in seven books: traditional count; the critical edition differs. Confirm phrasing.
Many scholars consider the Bala Kanda (and Uttara Kanda) later layers of the text; not mentioned in the script. Keeper may wish to add.
The payasa is divided unequally in Valmiki (half to Kausalya, portions to Sumitra and Kaikeyi, Sumitra twice), explaining the twins; simplified to 'divides it among the three'.
